blocks.text: Biodiversity, a term derived from biological diversity, refers to the variety of life forms present in different ecosystems. It encompasses the diversity of species, of genes and of ecosystems, and represents the richness and variability of living organisms and their interactions with each other and with their environments.

blocks.title: Ecosystem
blocks.text: An ecosystem is a dynamic and interactive system composed of living organisms and their physical environment. It includes all the biotic factors (the living things) as well as the abiotic factors (the non-living surroundings).

blocks.title: Niche
blocks.text: A niche is the role or function of an organism or species within an ecosystem. It includes its habitat, its interactions with other organisms (predation, competition and symbiosis) and its role in the flow of energy through the ecosystem.
Levels at which biodiversity is assessed
The assessment of biodiversity involves several levels, each giving its own insight into the complexity of life.

items: Species level: biodiversity is assessed by identifying and counting the different species present in an area. Species diversity includes not only the number of species but also their relative abundance and distribution.

Genetic level: biodiversity refers to the variety of genetic information carried by all the individual organisms of a species. Genetic diversity is crucial for the adaptability and survival of a species, because it lets the species cope with environmental changes and challenges.

Ecosystem level: the assessment covers the range of habitats, from forests and wetlands to grasslands and deserts. It involves understanding how different ecosystems function and how they contribute to overall ecological health.

blocks.text: Random sampling is a fundamental technique in ecological studies for assessing biodiversity within a specific area. It is crucial for five reasons.

items: It minimises bias: every part of the study area has an equal chance of being sampled, so the result represents the overall biodiversity more accurately.
It provides reliable estimates: the data can be analysed statistically to estimate species richness, abundance and distribution.
It facilitates comparisons: standardised methods of data collection allow different areas or habitats to be compared.
It enhances representativeness: by covering different parts of the study area, random sampling ensures that the sample represents the diversity of the whole area.
It supports conservation efforts: accurate assessments identify areas of high conservation value and allow changes in biodiversity to be monitored over time.

Quadrat sampling divides the study area into a grid and samples inside randomly selected squares, the quadrats. It suits plant populations and sessile organisms. For example, in a forest a researcher lays out quadrats of a fixed size and records the presence or absence of each plant species within them.

Transect sampling lays a line or strip (the transect) across the study area and records species at regular intervals along it. It is effective for studying how species are distributed across changing environments. For example, in a coastal zone a transect can run from the high-tide line to the low-tide line to record the types and abundance of intertidal organisms.

Aerial surveys use aircraft or drones to observe and record the distribution of organisms over large areas, for example to track bird species across a large wetland or to monitor large mammal populations in savannas.

blocks.alt: Three panels. Quadrat sampling: a field marked into a grid with a few squares shaded as the randomly chosen quadrats, each containing plant symbols to count. Transect sampling: a straight line running from the high-tide mark down a shore to the low-tide mark, with sample points at regular intervals. Aerial survey: a drone flying above a wetland, with flight lines drawn over the area.
blocks.caption: Three methods for assessing the distribution of organisms (original diagram after Figure 1.31).
blocks.long_description: Quadrats are fixed-size squares chosen at random on a grid. A transect is a line along which species are recorded at set intervals, often across a gradient such as a shore. An aerial survey covers a large area from above.

items: Point counts: an observer records the number of individuals of a species seen from a fixed point over a set period. This is commonly used for birds and other mobile animals.
Mark-recapture: individuals are captured, marked and released, then recaptured later to estimate population size and density. It is useful for animals that are difficult to count directly.
Quadrat counts: researchers count the individuals of a species inside each quadrat and use those counts to estimate overall abundance.
Capture-recapture models: these models allow for variables such as differing capture probabilities and movement between areas.
Remote sensing: satellite or drone imagery is used to assess the abundance and distribution of species, particularly over large or inaccessible areas.
